description: We’re building an interactive Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer to inspire the next generation of explorers! Our app will gamify real space science—from surviving on the Moon and Mars to managing space agriculture and mission data. We are looking for passionate teammates with skills in software development, data analysis/management, and planetary science. Join us to turn complex human spaceflight concepts into a fun, hands-on training adventure!
summary:
Every watt has a cost. Every breath is earned.
We developed a browser-based simulation engine and survival game for commanding a crewed Lunar or Martian outpost.
To address the challenge, our engine models true coupled life-support physics. Players balance solar and nuclear power, CO2 scrubbers, Sabatier reactors, hydroponics, and radiation shielding across two grueling missions: The Martian Dust Winter and Lunar Night at the South Pole Ridge. Every fix triggers a trade-off elsewhere, while dust storms, crew stress, and delayed Earth communications test real-time decision-making.
Space survival fails in cascades, yet most tools treat systems in isolation. Using seeded missions and an automated scientific debrief, entire classrooms can experience the exact same crisis and trace every failure to its root cause—delivering accessible, zero-server NASA-grade systems thinking to anyone with a browser.
details: Fix the air, freeze the crew. Save the power, starve the base. We built a browser-based simulation engine and strategy game that puts players in command of a crewed Lunar or Martian outpost. Unlike standard survival games with disconnected resource bars, our engine runs a true coupled Environmental Control and Life Support System (ECLSS). Power, air, water, heat, food, and radiation directly affect one another across twelve realistic subsystems—including solar arrays, nuclear reactors, batteries, CO2 scrubbers, water recyclers, electrolysis units, Sabatier reactors, hydroponics, radiator louvers, heaters, and regolith shielding. Players monitor individual crew health, stress, and radiation dose across two intense scenarios—The Martian Dust Winter and Lunar Night at the South Pole Ridge—while reacting to dust storms, solar particle events, micrometeorite strikes, and scaled communication delays from Earth.
